record.paper_title: Addition Machines, Automatic Functions and Open Problems of Floyd and Knuth
record.context_brief: outputting binary powers in subquadratic time
record.original_question: Given a natural number x as input to an integer addition machine, can the machine compute and output all powers of 2 that appear in the binary representation of x in subquadratic time o((log x)^2), with the powers allowed to be output in any order? For example, when x = 13, the desired output set is {8, 4, 1}.

evidence.quote: (5) Can the powers of 2 in the binary representation of x be computed and output by an integer addition machine in o((log x)2) steps?
For example, if x = 13, the program should output the numbers 8, 4, 1 in some order.

In Open Problem (5) they asked whether one can improve the runtime of an algorithm to output all powers of two appearing in the binary representation of a natural number in subquadratic time and the answer is that it can even be done in linear time.

artifact.self_contained_problem: An integer addition machine is a register machine operating on integer-valued registers whose elementary operations are: assigning a constant, copying a register, adding or subtracting one register from another, and conditional branching based on comparisons (<, =) of register contents; each such operation counts as one step. Given a natural number x supplied in an input register, design an integer addition machine that outputs (in any order, one per output step) exactly the set of powers of 2 appearing in the binary representation of x, i.e. the numbers 2^i for which the i-th bit of x equals 1. For instance, on input x = 13 the machine should output the three numbers 8, 4, 1 in some order. The question is: can such a machine be constructed whose running time on input x is o((log x)^2)?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem, originally posed as an open question by Floyd and Knuth, has been resolved: there is an integer addition machine that outputs all powers of two appearing in the binary representation of x in O(log x) (linear) time, which is in particular o((log x)^2).
